The establishment of a hyperacute rejection (HAR) model of ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation (ABOi-KTx) in nonhuman primates is of great significance for the study of the relevant clinical pathophysiological processes and related interventions in ABOi-KTx. In this study, blood group B cynomolgus monkeys were presensitized with synthetic blood group A-antigen conjugated to keyhole limpet hemocyanin (A-KLH) to boost circulating anti-A antibody levels. The serum anti-A antibody levels were measured by flow cytometry using type A human reagent red blood cells (RBCs) or monkey primary renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs) as target cells. ABOi-KTx was performed in type B monkeys using type A monkeys as donors. After 14 days of A-KLH sensitization, 12 of 16 (75%) type B monkeys had significantly elevated anti-A antibody levels. We found that in order to avoid irregular results in the detection of blood group antibodies by flow cytometry, it was more effective to use RTECs rather than RBCs as target cells. In the absence of presensitization, ABOi-KTx in three monkeys with relatively high levels of natural anti-A antibodies did not produce HAR. However, when four Type B monkeys with significantly increased anti-A antibodies after presensitization were randomly selected as recipients for ABOi-KTx, the allografts in all four monkeys developed HAR with typical pathologic characteristics. Thus, we have successfully established a monkey model of HAR in ABOi-KTx via blood group antigen presensitization, which will be helpful for the further study of rejection, accommodation, and clinical intervention in ABOi-KTx. ABO-incompatible renal transplantation hyperacute rejection blood group antibody flow cytometry non-human primate (NHP) National Natural Science Foundation of China 10.13039/501100001809 Introduction ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation (ABOi-KTx) is usually contraindicated because of the risk of hyperacute rejection (HAR) mediated by naturally occurring antibodies specific to donor blood group antigens ( 1 ). Nonetheless, unremitting donor organ shortages fuel attempts to cross the ABO barrier. ABOi-KTx has been shown to be safe, with acceptable long-term outcomes, when pretransplant desensitization strategies are used to reduce the accumulation of ABO blood group antibodies and B cells/plasma cells ( 2 – 4 ). Although some studies evaluating patient and graft outcome after ABOi-KTx have not shown any striking differences when compared with living donor ABO-compatible kidney transplantation (ABOc-KTx) ( 5 – 7 ), larger registry data have yielded conflicting results ( 8 – 10 ). Within the first 5 years after transplantation, ABOi-KTx is associated with a higher risk of mortality, loss of kidney grafts, infectious complications, and acute antibody-mediated rejection (AAMR) than is ABOc-KTx ( 10 ). In order to further elucidate the clinical pathophysiological processes involved in ABOi-KTx and to conduct related intervention studies, it is important to establish a clinically relevant nonhuman primate study model. Like humans, nonhuman primates express the ABH-specific antigens of the ABO histo-blood group system on the vascular endothelium, epithelial cells, and exocrine secretions ( 11 ). However, these ABH antigens are absent from or only weakly expressed on erythrocytes of both Old and New World monkeys ( 11 , 12 ). Baboons and macaques, two typical representatives of Old World monkeys, are frequently used in experimental transplantation research because of their physical traits and availability. Since the sera of baboons and macaques regularly contain naturally occurring anti-A and/or anti-B antibodies ( 11 , 13 ), the A and/or B antigens expressed on vascular endothelial and epithelial cells can be targets for immune rejection by a recipient ( 11 , 14 , 15 ), and they may exhibit a process of ABO-incompatible rejection similar to that seen in humans. The incidence of HAR has been estimated to be approximately 66% in humans that have received ABOi-KTx without any pretransplant desensitization treatment ( 16 , 17 ). In contrast, previous studies have shown that ABO incompatibility does not cause HAR in primate kidney transplant models ( 18 – 20 ), whereas it leads to early HAR in approximately 33% of baboon heart transplants ( 15 , 21 ). In order to achieve a high incidence of HAR, a presensitization strategy has been used to increase the levels of anti-A or anti-B antibodies in baboon recipients prior to ABO-incompatible cardiac transplantation ( 22 ), but there appear to be no data on successful HAR in a primate renal transplantation model between ABO-incompatible pairs. Therefore, in the present study we have presensitized blood type B recipient cynomolgus monkeys with synthetic blood group A antigen to establish a reliable nonhuman ABOi-KTx model in which all kidney allografts from blood type A donors undergo HAR. In addition, we have developed an improved flow cytometry technique for the detection of blood group antibody. We show that by using monkey primary renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs) expressing blood group antigen A rather than red blood cells (RBCs) as target cells, the serum levels of anti-blood group A antibodies can more accurately be evaluated by flow cytometry.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation (ABOi-KTx) with or without A-KLH presensitization, leading to hyperacute rejection (HAR) or other forms of rejection.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Hyperacute Rejection (HAR) in ABOi-KTx is mediated by elevated circulating anti-A antibodies, primarily IgM, specific to donor blood group antigens. Presensitization with A-KLH enhances immunogenicity, significantly increasing anti-A IgM and IgG levels to a threshold (e.g., IgM RMF > 30) sufficient to trigger HAR. HAR manifests as severe graft pathology, including interstitial hemorrhage, necrosis, intravascular thrombosis, and massive deposition of IgM, C3c, and C5b-9, with moderate IgG deposition. Without presensitization, HAR typically does not occur; instead, weaker antibody-mediated rejection (IgM, C3c, C5b-9 deposition) and cell-mediated rejection (CD3+, CD20+, CD68+ infiltration) may develop.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: ABOi-KTx without presensitization, even in monkeys with relatively high natural anti-A antibodies, did not induce Hyperacute Rejection (HAR), leading instead to weak antibody-mediated and cell-mediated rejection, with graft survival exceeding 30 days. In contrast, presensitization with A-KLH (e.g., 2 mg dose) significantly elevated anti-A antibody levels (in 75% of monkeys), resulting in 100% HAR in ABOi-KTx recipients. A minimum IgM antibody RMF > 30 is recommended for reliably inducing HAR. Additionally, using Monkey Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTECs) as target cells for flow cytometry provided more reliable and predictable antibody quantification across serum dilutions compared to human reagent Red Blood Cells (RBCs).
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The induction of hyperacute rejection (HAR) in ABOi-KTx is specifically dependent on significantly increased anti-A antibody levels achieved through presensitization, as natural antibody levels are generally insufficient in nonhuman primates. A-KLH presensitization specifically enhances these anti-A antibody levels, demonstrating its precise role in activating the adaptive immune response against blood group A antigens. Furthermore, Monkey Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTECs) offer superior specificity and reliability as target cells for flow cytometric anti-A antibody detection compared to human reagent RBCs, due to stable A antigen expression and predictable results.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Type B cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) serving as recipients for ABO-incompatible kidney transplants from type A donors, particularly those undergoing presensitization to elevate anti-A antibody levels. This model is clinically relevant for human patients undergoing ABOi-KTx.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation (ABOi-KTx) without desensitization carries significant risks including hyperacute rejection (HAR), acute antibody-mediated rejection (AAMR), graft loss, and mortality. The established nonhuman primate HAR model, achieved through A-KLH presensitization to significantly elevate anti-A antibody levels, is crucial for studying clinical pathophysiological processes of ABOi-KTx, severe renal failure, graft deterioration, and developing preventive/treatment strategies. This model demonstrates that elevated anti-A antibody levels directly lead to 100% incidence of HAR with severe graft pathology, while an improved assay for antibody monitoring offers diagnostic utility.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk, specifically hyperacute rejection (HAR) and acute antibody-mediated rejection (AAMR), leading to graft loss and mortality in ABOi-KTx. Diagnostic utility, through the monitoring of anti-A antibody levels using an improved flow cytometry assay.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Flow cytometry using type A human reagent Red Blood Cells (RBCs) as target cells for measuring anti-A IgM and IgG levels was found to be unreliable, yielding irregular, confusing, and unpredictable results (e.g., irregular Gmean, peaks, or cliffs), especially with high induced antibody levels or potential erythrocyte agglutination. In contrast, using monkey primary Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTECs) as target cells demonstrated superior reliability and effectiveness. RTECs stably express blood group A antigen, avoiding irregular results and providing clear, stratified distributions in flow cytometric antibody detection.
recommended_alternatives: monkey primary renal tubular epithelial cells (RTECs) as target cells for modified flow cytometric assay
Further study to determine whether vascular endothelial cells or RTECs are more suitable as target cells for anti-A antibody detection by flow cytometry, due to differences in A antigen expression
